title: Architectural innovation: Familiar components can displace incumbents
desc: Explains incumbent decline through changed component relationships and inherited evaluation criteria, not technological replacement or a universal causal law.

kps.k: Architectural innovation can undermine incumbents by changing how familiar components work together, rather than replacing their underlying concepts.
kps.d: In Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms, the authors use photolithographic equipment history to distinguish component expertise from knowledge of component relationships. Proximity alignment involved a modest conceptual change, but required a more accurate, stable gap-setting mechanism integrated differently with the rest of the equipment. Their central proposition is that established expertise can obstruct adaptation even when incumbents possess strong engineering capabilities and invest heavily.

qs.q: Thus, the successful design of a proximity aligner requires                 both the acquisition of some new component knowledge-                 how to build a more accurate and more stable gap-setting                 mechanism-and the acquisition of new architectural knowl-                 edge.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

qs.q: Since the accuracy and stability of the mechanism is as much                 a function of the way in which it is integrated with the other                 components as it is of its own design, the relationships be-                 tween the gap-setting mechanism and the other components                 of the aligner must change if the aligner is to perform well.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

kps.k: Inherited assessment criteria can prevent firms from recognising a new architecture's advantages.
kps.d: The authors interpret Kasper's difficulties as reliance on previously useful information filters, rather than simple carelessness. Kasper treated proximity alignment as a routine extension, attributed customer problems to processing errors and assessed Canon's equipment against contact-aligner criteria that obscured its redesigned gap mechanism. Perkin-Elmer likewise forecast individual component improvements accurately but missed how better resist systems and lens designs would jointly favour steppers. These cases challenge the assumption that accurate component-level analysis necessarily produces sound technology strategy.

qs.q: Like the incremental improvements to the con-                 tact aligner before it, design of the proximity aligner was                 managed as a routine extension to the product line.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

qs.q: In retrospect, this may seem like a wanton misuse of infor-                 mation, but it represented no more than a continued reliance                 on an information filter that had served the firm well histori-                 cally.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

kps.k: Recognising architectural change and implementing it pose distinct organisational problems.
kps.d: GCA's experience illustrates the implementation problem: component-based engineering teams and communication channels organised around its first-generation stepper struggled to understand Nikon's changed optical-system integration. Few engineers held responsibility for the relevant interactions, and GCA's second-generation machines fell short of market requirements. A practical implication of the analysis is that adaptation may require changing cross-team communication and responsibility for integration, not merely acquiring better components or increasing investment; the cases do not establish a tested organisational remedy.

qs.q: Part of the problem for GCA was recog-                nition, but much of its failure to master the new stepper                technology lay in problems in implementation.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

qs.q: GCA's engineers were orga-                nized by component, and cross-department communication                channels were all structured around the architecture of the                first-generation system.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

kps.k: The historical evidence supports a qualified explanation of incumbent decline, not a universal or single-cause account.
kps.d: The authors report recognition problems across four architectural transitions in this industry, but acknowledge that other factors contributed to the firms' market-share losses. Kasper also faced automatic-alignment, manufacturing and management problems. Continuing sales distort the supplied table's measure, especially for second-generation equipment still early in its life cycle in 1986. No competing source appears in the supplied material: the main qualifications come from the authors themselves. They describe organisational mirroring of product structure as an approximation and assume that knowledge embedded in routines becomes difficult to change. Applying this framework beyond photolithographic equipment therefore offers an analytical hypothesis, not direct evidence of outcomes in other sectors.

qs.q: Similar problems with recog-                 nition show up in all four episodes of architectural innovation                 in the industry's history.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

qs.q: In all three cases, other factors also                 played a role in the firm's dramatic loss of market share, but                 a failure to respond effectively to architectural innovation was                 of critical importance.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Its historical analysis argues that incumbent firms can be disadvantaged not by wholesale technological replacement, but by changes in how familiar components interact: inherited architectural knowledge, established evaluation filters and organisational arrangements can obscure those changes even where firms retain strong engineering capabilities and invest substantially. The source also distinguishes two mechanisms—failure to recognise the significance of a new architecture and failure to implement it through existing component-based teams and communication channels. Its internal qualifications do not make the position mixed: the authors treat architectural maladaptation as critically important rather than universally decisive or solely causal, acknowledge other contributors to market-share loss, and describe parts of their organisational theory as simplifying assumptions. Because the curated evidence contains one source in this professional voice, these findings characterise that source rather than academia and research generally.

qs.q: Our analysis of the industry's history suggests                that a reliance on architectural knowledge derived from expe-                rience with the previous generation blinded the incumbent                firms to critical aspects of the new technology.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

qs.q: In all three cases, other factors also                 played a role in the firm's dramatic loss of market share, but                 a failure to respond effectively to architectural innovation was                 of critical importance.
qs.a: Architectural Innovation: The Reconfiguration of Existing Product Technologies and the Failure of Established Firms · Academia · 1990

elens.an: The pre-2015 source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Its photolithographic-equipment cases argue that incumbents can be undermined when innovation changes relationships among otherwise familiar components: established architectural knowledge, inherited evaluation criteria and component-oriented organisational arrangements can obstruct both recognition and implementation, even where firms retain strong engineering capabilities and invest heavily. The source also supports the proposition’s deliberately qualified scope. It presents architectural maladaptation as critically important rather than universally determinative, acknowledges other contributors to market-share loss, identifies limitations in the historical measures, and characterises parts of its organisational theory as simplifying assumptions. Because this time-period facet contains one curated source, these findings establish that source’s alignment with the proposition, not the prevalence of the view among pre-2015 scholarship.
